title: The Contaminated Adult

source.quote: Eric Berne named these two problems contamination and exclusion.

setting: Thursday, 3pm. Victor, a consultant brought in to "fix hiring", has the room's full attention. He never once raises his voice.
playAs: Zoë, a colleague on the hiring panel

L1.line: Look, it's just a fact: people from that background don't test well under pressure, and honestly, I've never met one who could really hack this role anyway.
cues: delivered flat and confident, like a shared fact
no evidence offered, no counter-examples considered
"it's just a fact" used to shut down further checking
L1.question: Victor sounds calm and certain, like he's just reporting reality. What's actually going on?

options.text: This is real Adult reasoning - he's just being direct
options.feedback: Real Adult reasoning updates when checked and can point to evidence; "it's just a fact" used to end the conversation, with no evidence offered, is the opposite of that.

options.text: Parent contamination only - he's repeating a prejudice he was taught
options.feedback: There is a taught prejudice here ("people from that background don't test well") - but the second half, "I've never met one who could really hack this role", is his own experience generalized into certainty. There's more than one source feeding this.

options.text: Double contamination - a Parent prejudice and a Child delusion, both mistaken for fact
options.feedback: Right. "People from that background don't test well" is an inherited Parent prejudice; "I've never met one who could really hack this role" turns a handful of personal impressions into a sweeping belief, which is the Child-delusion half. Both get delivered in the same flat, certain Adult voice - that's what makes contamination dangerous: it doesn't sound like Parent or Child.

options.text: Child delusion only - he's generalizing from a few bad experiences
options.feedback: His own experience is doing some of the work, true - but "it's just a fact" about an entire group of people is also exactly the shape of an inherited prejudice, not something he worked out himself from scratch.

L1.lesson: Contamination is dangerous precisely because it doesn't come wearing a Parent scowl or a Child whine - it borrows the Adult's flat, reasonable voice. Berne's real test isn't the tone, it's the content: does this claim update when checked against reality, or does it just restate itself more firmly? Victor's claim does the second.

L2.intro: Three statements, three chances to test what's real Adult and what's borrowing its voice. You're on the panel - what do you say?

beats.line: Honestly, if people just worked harder, none of this would be an issue. That's just how the world works.

options.outcome: Victor's smile tightens. "I'm just stating facts." Now it's a standoff - certainty versus certainty.
options.lesson: Meeting a contaminated claim with a flat moral counter-claim from Controlling Parent doesn't expose the contamination, it just adds a second absolute to the room.

options.text: Can you point to the data behind that? I've seen the opposite in our own numbers.
options.outcome: Victor pauses. "Well - I mean, anecdotally..." For the first time, the certainty wobbles.
options.lesson: Asking for the evidence a real Adult claim should be able to produce tests contamination without attacking the person - if the claim can't survive the check, the Adult mask starts to slip on its own.

options.text: I guess that's probably true, you'd know better than me.
options.outcome: Victor nods, satisfied. The claim stands, reinforced, unchecked.
options.lesson: Accepting a contaminated claim because it was delivered with total confidence is exactly how prejudice gets passed on as "just facts" - the content is never actually tested.

options.text: Maybe, but let's focus on the hiring numbers instead.
options.outcome: The conversation moves on, but the claim itself is left standing, unchallenged, for next time.
options.lesson: Redirecting avoids a fight and keeps the meeting moving, but it leaves the contaminated belief completely intact for the next conversation.

beats.line: I don't even need to look at his resume - I can just tell within the first minute whether someone's going to work out. Never been wrong yet.
cues: no tracking of actual outcomes mentioned

options.outcome: Victor beams. "I know, right?" The delusion gets a round of applause.
options.lesson: Flattering an unfalsifiable claim ("never been wrong yet" - how would he know?) reinforces exactly the kind of overconfidence contamination runs on.

options.text: How would you actually know you've never been wrong - do you track the ones you rejected?
options.outcome: Victor opens his mouth, closes it. "I... no, not really." First real crack in the certainty all day.
options.lesson: This question goes straight at what makes "never been wrong yet" a Child delusion rather than an Adult conclusion: a real Adult claim can be checked against disconfirming cases, and this one never has been.

options.text: That's ridiculous, nobody can tell that fast.
options.outcome: Victor shrugs. "Twenty years of experience says otherwise." Dismissal doesn't dent confidence built this way.
options.lesson: A blunt dismissal from Parent gives Victor something to defend against rather than something to actually examine.

options.text: Sure, but let's still run the full process for this one.
options.outcome: Victor agrees, a little put out. The claim is sidestepped rather than tested, but the process stays intact for now.
options.lesson: Practical and safe for the hire, but the underlying delusion ("I can just tell") is never actually named or tested.

beats.line: Based on the last three cohorts' actual pass rates, candidates from bootcamps have underperformed on the systems-design round specifically - here's the breakdown.
cues: scoped to one round, not a sweeping claim

options.text: That's just prejudice dressed up in numbers.
options.outcome: Victor pulls up the actual spreadsheet. "It's... literally just the numbers." Crying contamination where there isn't any costs you credibility for the next real instance.
options.lesson: Treating every confident claim as contamination is its own trap - a claim backed by specific, checkable data and open to being wrong is exactly what real Adult content looks like; the diagnosis is in the evidence, not the confidence.

options.text: Interesting - what do you think is driving that gap, and what should we check before changing anything?
options.outcome: Victor relaxes slightly - a real question lands differently than a loaded one. "Honestly, I think it's the round's format, not the candidates. Worth testing."
options.lesson: Engaging real Adult content with more Adult content - curiosity, next steps, willingness to be wrong - is what distinguishes a genuine data-backed claim from the contaminated ones that only sound like it.

options.text: Okay, so bootcamp grads are a no, got it.
options.outcome: Victor frowns. "That's not what I said - it's one round, not a verdict on anyone." The data gets over-read into a blanket rule.
options.lesson: This over-generalizes a specific, limited finding into the same kind of sweeping claim contamination usually produces - ironically turning real Adult data into something that now behaves like a prejudice.

options.text: Let's just ignore that round's data for now.
options.outcome: Victor shrugs. "Your call," clearly unconvinced. Useful data gets shelved instead of used or checked.
options.lesson: Dismissing a genuinely checkable claim wastes real information - the skill here isn't suspicion of everything confident, it's testing each claim on its own merits.

fields.label: Draw the contamination: Victor's Parent prejudice and his Child delusion, both reaching into Adult.

There's a real pattern called "constant Adult exclusion" - someone who's genuinely shut the door on Parent and Child and runs on Adult alone, no feelings, no inherited rules, just cold processing. In under 60 words: Victor presents everything as flat, confident fact and never once says "I could be wrong" or asks a real question back - but he's contaminated, not excluded. Why is a contaminated Adult that successfully imitates constant-Adult exclusion more dangerous than the real thing?

echo.setting: 48 hours later: the hiring decision gets written up, and Victor's line from the first beat shows up verbatim in the official notes.
echo.line: If people just worked harder, none of this would be an issue.
echo.shape: same spot-the-contamination shape as L1, now as a written record instead of a spoken line
